message:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
Here's everything in order. Two things I couldn't answer exactly without more detail: your airline, for the bag check, and your dates, for the out-of-office message.

## Three things for a free evening

1. **Watch sunset from a miradouro (viewpoint).** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte has the widest view over the city. Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol, in Alfama, are closer to the centre and easy to combine with the next suggestion.
2. **Wander Alfama, then go to a fado house.** Alfama is the old Moorish quarter of steep lanes and small squares. Fado is Portugal's traditional mournful song, and Lisbon is its home. Smaller venues such as Tasca do Chico (in Bairro Alto) are more atmospheric than the big dinner-show places. Book or arrive early, and expect people to be quiet during the songs.
3. **Have dinner in Príncipe Real or Bairro Alto.** Try petiscos (Portuguese small plates), grilled fish, or bacalhau (salt cod). If you're short on time or energy, the Time Out Market at Cais do Sodré has many good stalls under one roof.

Lisbon is very hilly with slippery stone pavements, so wear proper shoes rather than work shoes. If you ride the famous Tram 28, watch for pickpockets.

## Saying "thank you"

- **Obrigado** if you're a man, **obrigada** if you're a woman.
- The form depends on the **speaker's** gender, not the gender of the person you're thanking. It literally means "obliged."
- *Muito obrigado/obrigada* means "thank you very much." The usual reply is *de nada* ("you're welcome").

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US, and nobody will mind if you don't. It's normal to round up, or to leave about 5–10% at a sit-down restaurant for good service. Cafés and quick meals need nothing beyond leaving the coins. Card machines often have no tip option, so a few euros in coins helps.

## Will your bag fit?

**That depends on the airline, and on your fare type.** Cabin bag rules vary a lot. Your bag is 56 × 36 × 23 cm and weighs 9 kg. Here's how it compares with some typical limits:

| Airline (typical economy limit) | Size | Weight | Your bag |
|---|---|---|---|
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 | 23 kg | ✅ Fits |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, if your fare includes one) | 56 × 45 × 25 | 15 kg | ✅ Fits |
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 23 | 8 kg | ⚠️ 1 cm too long, 1 kg too heavy |
| Lufthansa | 55 × 40 × 23 | 8 kg | ⚠️ Same as TAP |
| Ryanair (priority, large bag) | 55 × 40 × 20 | 10 kg | ❌ Too long and too deep |

These rules change, so check your airline's website and your booking. Basic fares often include only a small under-seat bag.

The weight limit is the likelier problem. **9 kg is over the common 8 kg limit**, and anything you buy will make you heavier on the way home. If your airline uses 8 kg, wear your heaviest shoes and your jacket on the plane, and move dense items like your laptop and chargers into your personal item. Tell me the airline and I can be more specific.

## Packing work shirts

**Fold, don't roll.** Rolling suits t-shirts and knitwear, but it leaves crisp cotton shirts creased.

- Button the shirt and fold the sleeves back. Fold it to roughly the size of an A4 sheet, with a sheet of tissue or a dry-cleaning bag inside to reduce friction.
- Stack the shirts flat on top of everything else, or put them in a packing folder.
- When you arrive, hang them up straight away. Steam from a hot shower in the bathroom will drop out most creases, and hotels usually have an iron on request.
- A travel-size wrinkle-release spray is handy, but it counts toward your liquids allowance.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling on business from [Wednesday 18] to [Friday 20 November] with limited access to email, so my replies may be slower than usual.
>
> I'll be back at my desk on [Monday 23 November] and will get back to you then. If your query is urgent, please contact [Name] at [email / phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

It works for clients because it's warm without oversharing, and it gives them a clear return date and a backup contact. Ask the colleague you name for permission first.

## Luggage tag colour

Choose something bright that few others will have: **neon orange, lime green, or hot pink**. Avoid black, navy and red, which are everywhere. Even when you travel carry-on only, a crowded flight can mean your bag is checked at the gate, so the tag still matters.

- Put your name, phone number and email on the tag rather than your home address.
- After losing a case in the spring, you might also want a tracker such as an AirTag inside the bag.

## Making the Friday return less stressful

- **Check in online exactly 24 hours ahead,** on Thursday evening, and save the boarding pass to your phone wallet. Set a reminder now.
- **Pack on Friday morning before your meetings.** Either check out and leave the bag at hotel reception, or bring it with you if your meetings allow.
- **Check your terminal.** Lisbon has Terminal 1 for most airlines and Terminal 2 for some low-cost carriers. Terminal 2 is reached by a shuttle bus from Terminal 1, so allow extra time if you're flying from there.
- **Getting to the airport.** The airport is close to the city. The metro's red line takes about 20–25 minutes from the centre and avoids traffic. A taxi or Uber is about 15–30 minutes, but Friday rush-hour traffic can double that.
- **Arrive about 2 hours before departure.** If you're flying out of the Schengen area, for example back to the UK, passport control at Lisbon can be slow, especially now that the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES) is in use. A bit more time is sensible.
- **Put your liquids bag and laptop on top** of your bag for security, and eat before boarding. You'll probably be hungry after a full day of meetings.

Have a great trip, and enjoy your first visit to Portugal!
